keep: He built bigger than anyone had asked. Britain kept the tunnel and the bridge, and narrowed the gauge in a weekend.
lede: His gauge lost in 1846, his atmospheric railway in 1848, and his biggest ship was sold off in 1864. A biography of 2005 calls him the man who built the world.
copy: Isambard Kingdom Brunel was born at Portsmouth on 9 April 1806, In 1826, when the engineer of the tunnel being dug under the Thames fell ill, the twenty-year-old Brunel took his place. In January 1828 he was working about 595 feet under the river when the earth broke in, through a hole the newspapers said was not more than six inches across. Six men died. He swam to the shaft, with injuries that kept him off the works for months. The tunnel opened in 1843, after nearly twenty years, and some 50,000 people walked through it in the first few days. The ramps for carriages were never built, for want of money. In 1831, at twenty-four, he was appointed engineer of a bridge over the Avon gorge at Clifton, estimated at £57,000.

As its engineer from 1833, he laid the Great Western Railway's track seven feet apart. On the narrow gauge, he told a royal commission, "the whole machine was too small for the work to be done". The commission heard forty-eight witnesses, thirty-five of them for the narrow gauge and four for the broad, all four Great Western men, Brunel among them. It agreed the broad gauge was faster and recommended the narrow one anyway, on cost. The Gauge Act of 18 August 1846 forbade new passenger lines on any other gauge, though it let the existing broad gauge stand, and made exceptions for lines in the west of England and South Wales. In August 1844 he recommended atmospheric propulsion for the South Devon Railway: trains moved by air pressure in a tube. Four years later, to the day, he recommended giving it up. Daniel Gooch, one of the four who had defended the broad gauge with him, called it, in memoirs quoted by R. A. Buchanan, "the greatest blunder that has been made in railways". Brunel paid up his own share of the losses, and refused his fees.

The Great Eastern was 692 feet long and, fitted out, six times the tonnage of any ship yet built. To save money he dropped the hydraulic gear he had planned for the launch; "from an unwise attempt to economise", he wrote to the directors in November 1857. When the ship moved, the winch handles spun, threw men into the air, and one of them died. "I may blame myself," he told the inquest. She was afloat in January 1858. On 5 September 1859 he collapsed with a stroke on board. Four days later, off Hastings, a heater exploded; a stop-cock fitted for a test had never been taken off. Six firemen died. On 15 September, so did he. She was sold in 1864 to lay telegraph cables. The Clifton bridge was finished in 1864 as his memorial, by other engineers, with secondhand chains. And over the weekend of 21 and 22 May 1892 the Great Western narrowed the last of his broad gauge to 4 feet 8½ inches.

bio.why: The counterweight to L. T. C. Rolt's life of 1957, the classic. Vaughan went back, his publisher says, to evidence that Rolt ignored or suppressed. Read his son's Life of 1870 for Brunel's own letters, and for the Gauge Commission's report, which the son printed while defending him.

contested: How to judge him, and some of the arithmetic. L. T. C. Rolt's biography of 1957 is the classic; Adrian Vaughan's of 1991 promised a genius who was also, in its publisher's words, "obstinate, unjust, dictatorial and in the end paranoid", from evidence Rolt had ignored. The Institution of Civil Engineers' own obituary in 1860 put it more gently: "his besetting fault was a seeking for novelty, where the adoption of a well-known model would have sufficed". On the atmospheric railway, R. A. Buchanan argued in Social Studies of Science (1992) that the decision was "daring but carefully calculated", undone by the problems of scaling up the pipe and its seal and by better steam locomotives. What it cost is disputed, and this house has read the figures only as Joseph Brennan reproduces them: a shareholder quoted by G. A. Sekon in 1895 put the spending at £300,000 to £400,000, with about £50,000 recovered by Sekon's count; Peter Kay's railway history of 1991 has £430,000 spent and about £85,000 recovered. On the gauge he was right about speed and lost on cost, which is a different thing from being wrong. Smaller counts disagree too. His son's Life has one death from the failed launch, other accounts two; Royal Museums Greenwich has six dead in the explosion, other accounts five. The Broad Gauge Society has 177 miles narrowed by 4,700 men in 1892, Mike Peart for the National Railway Museum's Friends 171 miles and 4,200 men.
